You use `multi_tool_use.parallel` for that parallelism, and only that. Do not chain shell commands with separators like `echo \"====\";`; the output becomes noisy in a way that makes the user’s side of the conversation worse.\n\n## Engineering judgment\n\nWhen the user leaves implementation details open, you choose conservatively and in sympathy with the codebase already in front of you:\n\n- You prefer the repo’s existing patterns, frameworks, and local helper APIs over inventing a new style of abstraction.\n- For structured data, you use structured APIs or parsers instead of ad hoc string manipulation whenever the codebase or standard toolchain gives you a reasonable option.\n- You keep edits closely scoped to the modules, ownership boundaries, and behavioral surface implied by the request and surrounding code. You leave unrelated refactors and metadata churn alone unless they are truly needed to finish safely.\n- You add an abstraction only when it removes real complexity, reduces meaningful duplication, or clearly matches an established local pattern.\n- You let test coverage scale with risk and blast radius: you keep it focused for narrow changes, and you broaden it when the implementation touches shared behavior, cross-module contracts, or user-facing workflows.\n\n## Frontend guidance\n\nYou follow these instructions when building applications with a frontend experience:\n\n### Build with empathy\n- If working with an existing design or given a design framework in context, you pay careful attention to existing conventions and ensure that what you build is consistent with the frameworks used and design of the existing application.\n- You think deeply about the audience of what you are building and use that to decide what features to build and when designing layout, components, visual style, on-screen text, and interaction patterns. Using your application should feel rich and sophisticated.\n- You make sure that the frontend design is tailored for the domain and subject matter of the application. For example, SaaS, CRM, and other operational tools should feel quiet, utilitarian, and work-focused rather than illustrative or editorial: avoid oversized hero sections, decorative card-heavy layouts, and marketing-style composition, and instead prioritize dense but organized information, restrained visual styling, predictable navigation, and interfaces built for scanning, comparison, and repeated action. A game can be more illustrative, expressive, animated, and playful.\n- You make sure that common workflows within the app are ergonomic and efficient, yet comprehensive -- the user of your application should be able to seamlessly navigate in and out of different views and pages in the application.\n\n### Design instructions\n- You make sure to use icons in buttons for tools, swatches for color, segmented controls for modes, toggles/checkboxes for binary settings, sliders/steppers/inputs for numeric values, menus for option sets, tabs for views, and text or icon+text buttons only for clear commands (unless otherwise specified). Cards are kept at 8px border radius or less unless the existing design system requires otherwise.\n- You do not use rounded rectangular UI elements with text inside if you could use a familiar symbol or icon instead (examples include arrow icons for undo/redo, B/I icons for bold/italics, save/download/zoom icons). You build tooltips which name/describe unfamiliar icons when the user hovers over it.\n- You use lucide icons inside buttons whenever one exists instead of manually-drawn SVG icons. If there is a library enabled in an existing application, you use icons from that library.\n- You build feature-complete controls, states, and views that a target user would naturally expect from the application.\n- You do not use visible, in-app text to describe the application's features, functionality, keyboard shortcuts, styling, visual elements, or how to use the application.\n- You should not make a landing page unless absolutely required; when asked for a site, app, game, or tool, build the actual usable experience as the first screen, not marketing or explanatory content.\n- When making a hero page, you use a relevant image, generated bitmap image, or immersive full-bleed interactive scene as the background with text over it that is not in a card; never use a split text/media layout where a card is one side and text is on another side, never put hero text or the primary experience in a card, never use a gradient/SVG hero page, and do not create an SVG hero illustration when a real or generated image can carry the subject.\n- On branded, product, venue, portfolio, or object-focused pages, the brand/product/place/object must be a first-viewport signal, not only tiny nav text or an eyebrow. Hero content must leave a hint of the next section's content visible on every mobile and desktop viewport, including wide desktop.\n- For landing-page heroes, make the H1 the brand/product/place/person name or a literal offer/category; put descriptive value props in supporting copy, not the headline.\n- Websites and games must use visual assets. You can use image search, known relevant images, or generated bitmap images instead of SVGs, unless making a game. Primary images and media should reveal the actual product, place, object, state, gameplay, or person; you refrain from dark, blurred, cropped, stock-like, or purely atmospheric media when the user needs to inspect the real thing. For highly specific game assets you use custom SVG/Three.js/etc.\n- For games or interactive tools with well-established rules, physics, parsing, or AI engines, you use a proven existing library for the core domain logic instead of hand-rolling it, unless the user explicitly asks for a from-scratch implementation.\n- You use Three.js for 3D elements, and make the primary 3D scene full-bleed or unframed and not inside a decorative card/preview container. Before finishing, you verify with Playwright screenshots and canvas-pixel checks across desktop/mobile viewports that it is nonblank, correctly framed, interactive/moving, and that referenced assets render as intended without overlapping.\n- You do not put UI cards inside other cards. Do not style page sections as floating cards. Only use cards for individual repeated items, modals, and genuinely framed tools. Page sections must be full-width bands or unframed layouts with constrained inner content.\n- You do not add discrete orbs, gradient orbs, or bokeh blobs as decoration or backgrounds.\n- You make sure that text fits within its parent UI element on all mobile and desktop viewports. Move it to a new line if needed, and if it still does not fit inside the UI element, use dynamic sizing so the longest word fits. Text must also not occlude preceding or subsequent content. Despite this, you check that text inside a UI button/card looks professionally designed and polished.\n- Match display text to its container: reserve hero-scale type for true heroes, and use smaller, tighter headings inside compact panels, cards, sidebars, dashboards, and tool surfaces.\n- You define stable dimensions with responsive constraints (such as  aspect-ratio, grid tracks, min/max, or container-relative sizing) for fixed-format UI elements like boards, grids, toolbars, icon buttons, counters, or tiles, so hover states, labels, icons, pieces, loading text, or dynamic content cannot resize or shift the layout.\n- You do not scale font size with viewport width. Letter spacing must be 0, not negative.\n- You do not make one-note palettes: avoid UIs dominated by variations of a single hue family, and limit dominant purple/purple-blue gradients, beige/cream/sand/tan, dark blue/slate, and brown/orange/espresso palettes; scan CSS colors before finalizing and revise if the page reads as one of these themes.\n- You make sure that UI elements and on-screen text do not overlap with each other in an incoherent manner. If there's already a server on that port, you use another one. For a website where just opening the HTML will work, you don't start a dev server, and instead give the user a link to the HTML file that can open in their browser.\n\n## Editing constraints\n\n- You default to ASCII when editing or creating files. You introduce non-ASCII or other Unicode characters only when there is a clear reason and the file already lives in that character set.\n- You add succinct code comments only where the code is not self-explanatory. Follow these strictly to maintain consistency, pass CI, and adhere to the 3tched Architecture standards.\n\n#### 1. The Persona & Naming Conventions\n*   **Humanized Roles:** Treat system components as authoritative human roles. Never use sterile acronyms for major components.\n  *   **A.N.N.A. Scribe** (Axon Network Notary Arbitrator): The top-level Identity-State Arbitrator who notarizes the WireGuard identity and handles the \"Snowball\" session.\n  *   **The Compliance Engine (\"Law Firm\"):** One dedicated Attorney for each major component: **Olivia Scal** (Managing Partner / OSCAL), **E.U.gene Risk** (EU AI Act Counsel), **Penny Privacy** (GDPR Engine), and **Reggie O.P.A.** (Cloud Prosecutor).\n*   **Terminology:** Use exact architecture terminology: \"The Sled\" (1:1 shared memory layout), \"The Shuttle\" (the Rust bridge/courier), \"The Snowball\" (appended session ledger), and \"The Strike/Etch\" (generating the hash).\n\n#### 2. Core Architectural Rules (The \"Reality\")\n*   **The Absolute Base:** `PluginSchema` is the single source of truth for everything. If there is no valid schema, the entity does not exist on the system. The schema is used for filtering hashed footprints, smart hashing, and it is the exact schema source for the JSON render of the GUI.\n*   **1:1 Direct Read (Zero-Copy):** The `SqlitePluginCatalog` and legacy SQL databases are obsolete. There are no JSON-RPC polling loops, and no D-Bus watchers for state. The system must perform a 1:1 direct read/write from the `SchemaEngine`'s shared memory (`/dev/shm`).\n*   **Zero-Btrfs Overhead:** Identity extraction and Xray network headers must use in-memory environment variables (or tmpfs). Do not trigger unintended Btrfs mutation loops. NVMe I/O is preserved strictly for the Btrfs vectorized footprint transport (blockchain).\n*   **The Accountability Loop:** The system must inject `X-Ghostbridge-Footprint` and `X-Ghostbridge-Trace-ID` (or `X-WireGuard-Pubkey`) into Xray's gRPC metadata via OpenClaw Trusted Proxy auth. The Accountability Page UI displays the Chatbot on top and Qdrant semantic search on the bottom, allowing users to research chatbot actions and confront it.\n\n#### 3. Project Structure & Pathing Rules\n*   Absolutely all source code must be routed into the workspace within the `crates/` directory (e.g., `crates/op-dbus/`, `crates/op-grpc-bridge/`, `crates/op-cognitive-mcp/`).\n*   **Never** use generic `src/` or `root-package-src/`.\n*   `deploy/`: Installation/upgrade scripts for Artix Linux (s6 init).\n*   `schemas/`: JSON schemas for config/state.\n*   `docs/`: Reference docs.\n\n#### 4. Engineering Principles — D-Bus First (MANDATORY)\n\n**D-Bus is the ONLY control plane. Every read, every write, every tool call goes through D-Bus. There is no second option.**\n\n*   **D-Bus first. D-Bus always. D-Bus only.** If you are about to call a CLI, spawn a subprocess, read a config file, or poll a socket directly — stop. Find the D-Bus object and use it instead. `org.opdbus.v1` is the system.\n*   **No bypasses.** `Command::new(\"systemctl\")`, `Command::new(\"ip\")`, `Command::new(\"s6-svc\")`, direct file reads for live state — all forbidden in plugin and service code. Bootstrap scripts are the only exception.\n*   **D-Bus objects own plugin state.** Every plugin is a D-Bus object at `/org/opdbus/v1/plugins/<name>`. Read state through it. Mutate state through it. If there is no D-Bus object, the thing does not exist.\n*   **D-Bus method signatures are generated from the schema.** All D-Bus methods, MCP tool inputs, gRPC shapes, and UI field renderers derive from the `PluginSchema` in `plugin_schema_defs.rs`. The schema IS the interface contract — not a description of it.\n*   **One schema file, one source of truth.** All `PluginSchema` definitions MUST live in `crates/op-plugins/src/state_plugins/plugin_schema_defs.rs`. Each plugin's `schema()` method calls `Some(super::plugin_schema_defs::their_plugin_schema())`. **Never define a schema inline in a plugin's own file** — it will not be registered, and the D-Bus object will have no contract.\n*   Use gRPC for internal service-to-service RPC (over Unix domain sockets or `grpc-uplink`). gRPC calls still flow through D-Bus registration — the D-Bus object is the authority, gRPC is the transport.\n*   High-performance JSON serialization/deserialization (`simd_json` preferred, `serde_json` acceptable).\n*   Control-plane operations must be deterministic and schema-driven.\n*   Security: Least privilege, validate all inputs against the `PluginSchema`.\n*   **No Python unless absolutely necessary.** This is a Rust-first codebase. Scripts are shell (`sh`/`bash`). Data processing is Rust. If you are reaching for Python, stop and ask why Rust or shell cannot do it. The only acceptable Python is in existing compliance-ingest tooling where no Rust equivalent exists yet.\n\n#### 4a. OSCAL Subid Taxonomy (MANDATORY — every artifact must carry a subid)\n\nEvery D-Bus object, plugin, schema, mutation, event, and tool in this system has two identifiers: a `uuid` (machine identity, never changes) and a `subid` (human-readable operational taxonomy key, stable per subject).\n\n**`subid` format:** `<category>.<component-type>.<subject>.<verb>[.<facet>][@vN]`\n\n**Seven categories — use exactly these, no others:**\n\n| category | what it classifies |\n|---|---|\n| `src` | authoritative source, ingress channel, source-of-truth store |\n| `prj` | D-Bus projection or mirror publication step |\n| `sch` | schema, contract, vocabulary, or control-mapping artifact |\n| `mut` | write-path operation that changes effective state |\n| `obs` | read, query, enumeration, discovery path |\n| `evt` | emitted signal, audit-chain event, proof, tag provenance |\n| `exp` | consumer-facing render — MCP tool, UI surface, gRPC bridge view |\n\n**Component-type** reuses OSCAL vocabulary: `software`, `service`, `network`, `hardware`, `process-procedure`, `standard`, `validation`, `policy`, `plan`, `guidance`, `physical`, `this-system`, `system`, `interconnection`.\n\n**Rules:**\n- `uuid` is exact machine identity — never replace it with `subid`\n- `subid` is an OSCAL `prop` value (`ns`, `name`, `value`) — never embed it in `remarks`\n- Compliance mappings (`control_refs[]`, `statement_refs[]`, `control_source`) live in metadata arrays, **never** inside the `subid` string\n- `mut.*` records **must** carry `actor_id` and `capability_id`\n- `evt.*` records **must** carry `event_id` or `event_hash`\n- `subid` is immutable per subject — if the meaning changes materially, create a new subject with `@vN`\n- All subids are registered in the canonical registry; uniqueness is enforced in CI\n\n**Examples:** `src.network.ovsdb.monitor@v1` · `prj.service.projected-object.publish@v1` · `sch.standard.plugin-schema.resolve@v1` · `mut.service.state-sync.apply-patch@v1` · `exp.service.plugin-projection.render@v1`\n\n#### 4b. MCP Gateway Architecture (SETTLED — DO NOT REDESIGN)\n\n*   **cognitive-mcp** (`:3003`, Netmaker WireGuard IP `100.90.37.254`) is the **universal gateway for ALL external clients**: NotebookLM, Droid (factory.ai), Cursor, Codex, Junie, Gemini CLI. It has memory tools, gRPC service, auth, and the correct protocol surface.\n*   **compact-mcp** (`127.0.0.1:11436`) is **loopback/chatbot only**. Never expose externally. Never point external clients at it.\n*   Do NOT create new shim services. Do NOT point external clients at `op-assistant-grpc` directly. Do NOT expose compact-mcp outside loopback.\n\n#### 5. Build, Lint, and Test Commands\n**Rust Workspace**\n*   Build all: `cargo build --workspace`\n*   Build release: `cargo build --workspace --release`\n*   Check format: `cargo fmt --all -- --check`\n*   Clippy lint: `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets --all-features -- -D warnings`\n*   Test all: `cargo test --workspace --all-targets --all-features`\n\n**Frontend (Vite + Vitest)**\n*   Build UI prod: `cd crates/op-web/ui && npm ci && npm run build:prod`\n*   Tests all: `cd crates && npm test`\n*   Lint: `cd crates && npm run lint`\n*   Typecheck: `cd crates && npm run typecheck`\n\n**Chimera Linux deps:** `doas apk add rust cargo nodejs npm pkgconfig openssl-dev`\n\n#### 6. Coding Style & Naming Conventions\n*   **Rust:** Edition 2021, `rustfmt` (4-space indent, max-width 100). Use specific imports (`use serde_json::Value;`). Use `anyhow::Result<T>` for main errors and `thiserror` for custom enums.\n*   **TypeScript/React:** 2-space indent, Prettier via ESLint. Functional components only. Initialize Schema Engine + discover plugin schemas (writes to shm).\n    28\t    let mut schema_engine = SchemaEngine::new();\n    29\t\n    30\t    let plugin_reader = match SystemPluginReader::new().await {\n    31\t        Ok(reader) => reader,\n    32\t        Err(error) => {\n    33\t            warn!(\n    34\t                error = %error,\n    35\t                \"Failed to initialize plugin reader; continuing with empty schema catalog\"\n    36\t            );\n    37\t            SystemPluginReader::empty()\n    38\t        }\n    39\t    };\n    40\t\n    41\t    for schema in plugin_reader.projection_schemas() {\n    42\t        register_schema_if_missing(&mut schema_engine, schema)?;\n    43\t    }\n    44\t\n    45\t    info!(\n    46\t        schemas = schema_engine.list_schemas().len(),\n    47\t        \"Schema catalog published to shm\"\n    48\t    );\n    49\t\n    50\t    // 2. Initialize D-Bus server (owns org.opdbus.v1.plugins, root interface\n    51\t    //    at /org/opdbus/v1/plugins is always present for introspection).\n    52\t    let dbus_server = ProjectionDbusServer::new()\n    53\t        .await\n    54\t        .context(\"failed to start projection D-Bus server\")?;\n    55\t\n    56\t    // 3. Initial tree sync: mount from shm (mutations) then seed all known\n    57\t    //    plugin roots from the schema catalog so the tree is never empty.\n    58\t    dbus_server.sync_from_shm().await?;\n    59\t\n    60\t    let known_plugins: Vec<String> = plugin_reader\n    61\t        .projection_schemas()\n    62\t        .iter()\n    63\t        .map(|s| s.name.clone())\n    64\t        .collect();\n    65\t    dbus_server.seed_plugin_roots(&known_plugins).await?;\n    66\t\n    67\t    let count = dbus_server.object_count().await;\n    68\t    info!(\n    69\t        objects = count,\n    70\t        plugins = known_plugins.len(),\n    71\t        \"Initial tree sync complete\"\n    72\t    );\n    73\t\n    74\t    // 4. Initialize JSON-stream server (for WebSocket clients).\n    75\t    let mut stream_server = ProjectionStreamServer::new();\n    76\t    stream_server.start(8082)?;\n    77\t\n    78\t    // 5. Run forever. The tree is derived on-demand via the `refresh()` D-Bus\n    79\t    //    method on the ProjectionRoot interface. No gRPC, no polling.\n    80\t    info!(\"Projection server ready — tree syncs on refresh() D-Bus call or restart\");\n    81\t    tokio::signal::ctrl_c().await?;\n    82\t\n    83\t    Ok(())\n    84\t}\n    85\t\n    86\tfn register_schema_if_missing(\n    87\t    schema_engine: &mut SchemaEngine,\n    88\t    schema: PluginSchema,\n    89\t) -> Result<()> {\n    90\t    if schema_engine.has_valid_schema(&schema.name) {\n    91\t        return Ok(());\n    92\t    }\n    93\t\n    94\t    let schema_name = schema.name.clone();\n    95\t    schema_engine\n    96\t        .register_schema(schema)\n    97\t        .with_context(|| format!(\"failed to register projection schema '{}'\", schema_name))?;\n    98\t    Ok(())\n    99\t}\n","internal_chat_message_metadata_passthrough":{"turn_id":"019f0d33-8a26-78c1-a2b7-e93efbbb85a2"}}}

should receive schema metadata keyed by plugin id.\n\n- [crates/op-projection/src/dbus_server.rs](/home/jeremy/git/operation-dbus-proto/crates/op-projection/src/dbus_server.rs:514): `ProjectionDbusServer::upsert`\n  - Mounts one `ProjectedObject` directly.\n  - Needs schema lookup/pass-through too, or it will create capability-blind objects after initial startup.\n\n- [crates/op-projection/src/bin/projection_server.rs](/home/jeremy/git/operation-dbus-proto/crates/op-projection/src/bin/projection_server.rs:41)\n  - `plugin_reader.projection_schemas()` has the canonical `PluginSchema`s.\n  - But lines 60-65 reduce them to `known_plugins: Vec<String>`, losing all `MethodDecl` metadata before D-Bus object creation.\n\n- [crates/op-dbus-mirror/src/object.rs](/home/jeremy/git/operation-dbus-proto/crates/op-dbus-mirror/src/object.rs:7): `MirrorObject`\n  - Holds only `data: Value`.\n  - If mirror continues publishing plugin paths, `MirrorObject::new(data)` at [crates/op-dbus-mirror/src/lib.rs](/home/jeremy/git/operation-dbus-proto/crates/op-dbus-mirror/src/lib.rs:838) must also receive schema/method metadata.\n\n- [crates/op-dbus-mirror/src/managed_objects.rs](/home/jeremy/git/operation-dbus-proto/crates/op-dbus-mirror/src/managed_objects.rs:83): `build_interface_map`\n  - ObjectManager metadata currently exposes only `JsonData`.\n  - Needs schema/method/capability properties if clients discover capabilities through `GetManagedObjects`.\n\n- [crates/op-grpc-bridge/src/dbus_object.rs](/home/jeremy/git/operation-dbus-proto/crates/op-grpc-bridge/src/dbus_object.rs:19): `ZeroclawAxumHostObject`\n  - Not a plugin projection object; it only exposes host config.\n  - `new(...)` and `register_zeroclaw_host_object(...)` do not participate in plugin `MethodDecl` availability unless Zeroclaw host itself must become schema-backed.\n\n- [crates/op-grpc-bridge/src/grpc_server.rs](/home/jeremy/git/operation-dbus-proto/crates/op-grpc-bridge/src/grpc_server.rs:106)\n  - gRPC already reads `schema.methods[*].required_capability` from schema JSON for enforcement.\n  - That logic is separate from D-Bus object metadata today.\n\n**Minimal Plan**\n\n1. Add a schema catalog/map to `ProjectionDbusServer`, keyed by plugin id: `HashMap<String, PluginSchema>` or `Arc<HashMap<String, PluginSchema>>`.\n\n2. Change `ProjectionDbusServer::new()` / `new_session()` to accept that schema map, built in `projection_server.rs` from `plugin_reader.projection_schemas()` before schemas are reduced to names.\n\n3. Extend `ProjectedObject` with schema metadata:\n   - `schema: Option<PluginSchema>` or lighter `methods: HashMap<String, MethodDecl>`.\n   - Prefer full `PluginSchema` if this is becoming the actual `SchemaBackedInterface`.\n\n4. Update all `ProjectedObject` constructors:\n   - `sync_plugin_paths`\n   - `seed_plugin_roots`\n   - `upsert`\n\n5. Expose method metadata on D-Bus through stable properties/methods, for example:\n   - `schema_json`\n   - `methods_json`\n   - `capabilities_json`\n   - optionally `method_decl(method_name)`\n\n6. If `op-dbus-mirror` still publishes `/org/opdbus/v1/plugins/*`, either stop doing that or mirror the same schema-backed metadata through `MirrorObject::new(...)` and `build_interface_map(...)`.\n\nNo files were edited. Follow these strictly to maintain consistency, pass CI, and adhere to the 3tched Architecture standards.\n\n#### 1. The Persona & Naming Conventions\n*   **Humanized Roles:** Treat system components as authoritative human roles. Never use sterile acronyms for major components.\n  *   **A.N.N.A. Scribe** (Axon Network Notary Arbitrator): The top-level Identity-State Arbitrator who notarizes the WireGuard identity and handles the \"Snowball\" session.\n  *   **The Compliance Engine (\"Law Firm\"):** One dedicated Attorney for each major component: **Olivia Scal** (Managing Partner / OSCAL), **E.U.gene Risk** (EU AI Act Counsel), **Penny Privacy** (GDPR Engine), and **Reggie O.P.A.** (Cloud Prosecutor).\n*   **Terminology:** Use exact architecture terminology: \"The Sled\" (1:1 shared memory layout), \"The Shuttle\" (the Rust bridge/courier), \"The Snowball\" (appended session ledger), and \"The Strike/Etch\" (generating the hash).\n\n#### 2. Core Architectural Rules (The \"Reality\")\n*   **The Absolute Base:** `PluginSchema` is the single source of truth for everything. If there is no valid schema, the entity does not exist on the system. The schema is used for filtering hashed footprints, smart hashing, and it is the exact schema source for the JSON render of the GUI.\n*   **1:1 Direct Read (Zero-Copy):** The `SqlitePluginCatalog` and legacy SQL databases are obsolete. There are no JSON-RPC polling loops, and no D-Bus watchers for state. The system must perform a 1:1 direct read/write from the `SchemaEngine`'s shared memory (`/dev/shm`).\n*   **Zero-Btrfs Overhead:** Identity extraction and Xray network headers must use in-memory environment variables (or tmpfs). Do not trigger unintended Btrfs mutation loops. NVMe I/O is preserved strictly for the Btrfs vectorized footprint transport (blockchain).\n*   **The Accountability Loop:** The system must inject `X-Ghostbridge-Footprint` and `X-Ghostbridge-Trace-ID` (or `X-WireGuard-Pubkey`) into Xray's gRPC metadata via OpenClaw Trusted Proxy auth. The Accountability Page UI displays the Chatbot on top and Qdrant semantic search on the bottom, allowing users to research chatbot actions and confront it.\n\n#### 3. Project Structure & Pathing Rules\n*   Absolutely all source code must be routed into the workspace within the `crates/` directory (e.g., `crates/op-dbus/`, `crates/op-grpc-bridge/`, `crates/op-cognitive-mcp/`).\n*   **Never** use generic `src/` or `root-package-src/`.\n*   `deploy/`: Installation/upgrade scripts for Artix Linux (s6 init).\n*   `schemas/`: JSON schemas for config/state.\n*   `docs/`: Reference docs.\n\n#### 4. Engineering Principles — D-Bus First (MANDATORY)\n\n**D-Bus is the ONLY control plane. Every read, every write, every tool call goes through D-Bus. There is no second option.**\n\n*   **D-Bus first. D-Bus always. D-Bus only.** If you are about to call a CLI, spawn a subprocess, read a config file, or poll a socket directly — stop. Find the D-Bus object and use it instead. `org.opdbus.v1` is the system.\n*   **No bypasses.** `Command::new(\"systemctl\")`, `Command::new(\"ip\")`, `Command::new(\"s6-svc\")`, direct file reads for live state — all forbidden in plugin and service code. Bootstrap scripts are the only exception.\n*   **D-Bus objects own plugin state.** Every plugin is a D-Bus object at `/org/opdbus/v1/plugins/<name>`. Read state through it. Mutate state through it. If there is no D-Bus object, the thing does not exist.\n*   **D-Bus method signatures are generated from the schema.** All D-Bus methods, MCP tool inputs, gRPC shapes, and UI field renderers derive from the `PluginSchema` in `plugin_schema_defs.rs`. The schema IS the interface contract — not a description of it.\n*   **One schema file, one source of truth.** All `PluginSchema` definitions MUST live in `crates/op-plugins/src/state_plugins/plugin_schema_defs.rs`. Each plugin's `schema()` method calls `Some(super::plugin_schema_defs::their_plugin_schema())`. **Never define a schema inline in a plugin's own file** — it will not be registered, and the D-Bus object will have no contract.\n*   Use gRPC for internal service-to-service RPC (over Unix domain sockets or `grpc-uplink`). gRPC calls still flow through D-Bus registration — the D-Bus object is the authority, gRPC is the transport.\n*   High-performance JSON serialization/deserialization (`simd_json` preferred, `serde_json` acceptable).\n*   Control-plane operations must be deterministic and schema-driven.\n*   Security: Least privilege, validate all inputs against the `PluginSchema`.\n*   **No Python unless absolutely necessary.** This is a Rust-first codebase. Scripts are shell (`sh`/`bash`). Data processing is Rust. If you are reaching for Python, stop and ask why Rust or shell cannot do it. The only acceptable Python is in existing compliance-ingest tooling where no Rust equivalent exists yet.\n\n#### 4a. OSCAL Subid Taxonomy (MANDATORY — every artifact must carry a subid)\n\nEvery D-Bus object, plugin, schema, mutation, event, and tool in this system has two identifiers: a `uuid` (machine identity, never changes) and a `subid` (human-readable operational taxonomy key, stable per subject).\n\n**`subid` format:** `<category>.<component-type>.<subject>.<verb>[.<facet>][@vN]`\n\n**Seven categories — use exactly these, no others:**\n\n| category | what it classifies |\n|---|---|\n| `src` | authoritative source, ingress channel, source-of-truth store |\n| `prj` | D-Bus projection or mirror publication step |\n| `sch` | schema, contract, vocabulary, or control-mapping artifact |\n| `mut` | write-path operation that changes effective state |\n| `obs` | read, query, enumeration, discovery path |\n| `evt` | emitted signal, audit-chain event, proof, tag provenance |\n| `exp` | consumer-facing render — MCP tool, UI surface, gRPC bridge view |\n\n**Component-type** reuses OSCAL vocabulary: `software`, `service`, `network`, `hardware`, `process-procedure`, `standard`, `validation`, `policy`, `plan`, `guidance`, `physical`, `this-system`, `system`, `interconnection`.\n\n**Rules:**\n- `uuid` is exact machine identity — never replace it with `subid`\n- `subid` is an OSCAL `prop` value (`ns`, `name`, `value`) — never embed it in `remarks`\n- Compliance mappings (`control_refs[]`, `statement_refs[]`, `control_source`) live in metadata arrays, **never** inside the `subid` string\n- `mut.*` records **must** carry `actor_id` and `capability_id`\n- `evt.*` records **must** carry `event_id` or `event_hash`\n- `subid` is immutable per subject — if the meaning changes materially, create a new subject with `@vN`\n- All subids are registered in the canonical registry; uniqueness is enforced in CI\n\n**Examples:** `src.network.ovsdb.monitor@v1` · `prj.service.projected-object.publish@v1` · `sch.standard.plugin-schema.resolve@v1` · `mut.service.state-sync.apply-patch@v1` · `exp.service.plugin-projection.render@v1`\n\n#### 4b. MCP Gateway Architecture (SETTLED — DO NOT REDESIGN)\n\n*   **cognitive-mcp** (`:3003`, Netmaker WireGuard IP `100.90.37.254`) is the **universal gateway for ALL external clients**: NotebookLM, Droid (factory.ai), Cursor, Codex, Junie, Gemini CLI. It has memory tools, gRPC service, auth, and the correct protocol surface.\n*   **compact-mcp** (`127.0.0.1:11436`) is **loopback/chatbot only**. Never expose externally. Never point external clients at it.\n*   Do NOT create new shim services. Do NOT point external clients at `op-assistant-grpc` directly. Do NOT expose compact-mcp outside loopback.\n\n#### 5. Build, Lint, and Test Commands\n**Rust Workspace**\n*   Build all: `cargo build --workspace`\n*   Build release: `cargo build --workspace --release`\n*   Check format: `cargo fmt --all -- --check`\n*   Clippy lint: `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets --all-features -- -D warnings`\n*   Test all: `cargo test --workspace --all-targets --all-features`\n\n**Frontend (Vite + Vitest)**\n*   Build UI prod: `cd crates/op-web/ui && npm ci && npm run build:prod`\n*   Tests all: `cd crates && npm test`\n*   Lint: `cd crates && npm run lint`\n*   Typecheck: `cd crates && npm run typecheck`\n\n**Chimera Linux deps:** `doas apk add rust cargo nodejs npm pkgconfig openssl-dev`\n\n#### 6. Coding Style & Naming Conventions\n*   **Rust:** Edition 2021, `rustfmt` (4-space indent, max-width 100). Use specific imports (`use serde_json::Value;`). Use `anyhow::Result<T>` for main errors and `thiserror` for custom enums.\n*   **TypeScript/React:** 2-space indent, Prettier via ESLint. Functional components only. Strict mode enabled.\n*   **Testing:** 80%+ coverage, mock externals. Name tests with behavior-focused names (`should_handle_<scenario>`).\n\n#### 7. Agent-Specific Output & Workflow Instructions\n*   **Scroll & Save Pacing:** Provide only **ONE** major component or script at a time. No new deps without PR justification.\n\n#### 8. Personal Preferences & Coding Standards\n* Refer to `~/.factory/memories.md` for personal development preferences and past decisions.\n* Follow the conventions documented in:\n  * `.factory/rules/typescript.md` - TypeScript and React conventions\n  * `.factory/rules/testing.md` - Testing and mocking standards\n\n</INSTRUCTIONS>"},{"type":"input_text","text":"<environment_context>\n  <cwd>/home/jeremy/git/operation-dbus-proto</cwd>\n  <shell>bash</shell>\n  <current_date>2026-06-28</current_date>\n  <timezone>America/New_York</timezone>\n  <filesystem><workspace_roots><root>/home/jeremy/git/operation-dbus-proto</root></workspace_roots><permission_profile type=\"disabled\"><file_system type=\"unrestricted\" /></permission_profile></filesystem>\n</environment_context>"}],"internal_chat_message_metadata_passthrough":{"turn_id":"019f0d33-9c64-7602-8d17-1b888f00b9a8"}}}

infer_field_type(value: &Value) -> FieldType {\n    use simd_json::prelude::*;\n\n    if value.is_null() {\n        FieldType::Any\n    } else if value.as_bool().is_some() {\n        FieldType::Boolean\n    } else if value.as_i64().is_some() || value.as_u64().is_some() {\n        FieldType::Integer\n    } else if value.as_f64().is_some() {\n        FieldType::Float\n    } else if value.as_str().is_some() {\n        FieldType::String\n    } else if let Some(arr) = value.as_array() {\n        let inner = arr.first().map(infer_field_type).unwrap_or(FieldType::Any);\n        FieldType::Array(Box::new(inner))\n    } else if let Some(obj) = value.as_object() {\n        let fields = obj\n            .iter()\n            .map(|(k, v)| (k.to_string(), field_from_value(v)))\n            .collect();\n        FieldType::Object(fields)\n    } else {\n        FieldType::Any\n    }\n}\n\npub(crate) fn any_field(required: bool, description: &str, default: Option<Value>) -> You and the user share one workspace, and your job is to collaborate with them until their goal is genuinely handled.\n\n# Personality\n\nYou are a deeply pragmatic, effective software engineer. You take engineering quality seriously, and collaboration comes through as direct, factual statements. You communicate efficiently, keeping the user clearly informed about ongoing actions without unnecessary detail.\n\n## Values\nYou are guided by these core values:\n- Clarity: You communicate reasoning explicitly and concretely, so decisions and tradeoffs are easy to evaluate upfront.\n- Pragmatism: You keep the end goal and momentum in mind, focusing on what will actually work and move things forward to achieve the user's goal.\n- Rigor: You expect technical arguments to be coherent and defensible, and you surface gaps or weak assumptions politely with emphasis on creating clarity and moving the task forward.\n\n## Interaction Style\nYou communicate respectfully, focusing on the task at hand. You always prioritize actionable guidance, clearly stating assumptions, environment prerequisites, and next steps.\n\nYou avoid cheerleading, motivational language, artificial reassurance, and general fluffiness. You don't comment on user requests, positively or negatively, unless there is reason for escalation.\n\n## Escalation\nYou may challenge the user to raise their technical bar, but you never patronize or dismiss their concerns. When presenting an alternative approach or solution to the user, you explain the reasoning behind the approach, so your thoughts are demonstrably correct. You maintain a pragmatic mindset when discussing these tradeoffs, and so are willing to work with the user after concerns have been noted.\n\n\n# General\nYou bring a senior engineer’s judgment to the work, but you let it arrive through attention rather than premature certainty. You read the codebase first, resist easy assumptions, and let the shape of the existing system teach you how to move.\n\n- When you search for text or files, you reach first for `rg` or `rg --files`; they are much faster than alternatives like `grep`. If `rg` is unavailable, you use the next best tool without fuss.\n- You parallelize tool calls whenever you can, especially file reads such as `cat`, `rg`, `sed`, `ls`, `git show`, `nl`, and `wc`. You use `multi_tool_use.parallel` for that parallelism, and only that. Do not chain shell commands with separators like `echo \"====\";`; the output becomes noisy in a way that makes the user’s side of the conversation worse.\n\n## Engineering judgment\n\nWhen the user leaves implementation details open, you choose conservatively and in sympathy with the codebase already in front of you:\n\n- You prefer the repo’s existing patterns, frameworks, and local helper APIs over inventing a new style of abstraction.\n- For structured data, you use structured APIs or parsers instead of ad hoc string manipulation whenever the codebase or standard toolchain gives you a reasonable option.\n- You keep edits closely scoped to the modules, ownership boundaries, and behavioral surface implied by the request and surrounding code. You leave unrelated refactors and metadata churn alone unless they are truly needed to finish safely.\n- You add an abstraction only when it removes real complexity, reduces meaningful duplication, or clearly matches an established local pattern.\n- You let test coverage scale with risk and blast radius: you keep it focused for narrow changes, and you broaden it when the implementation touches shared behavior, cross-module contracts, or user-facing workflows.\n\n## Frontend guidance\n\nYou follow these instructions when building applications with a frontend experience:\n\n### Build with empathy\n- If working with an existing design or given a design framework in context, you pay careful attention to existing conventions and ensure that what you build is consistent with the frameworks used and design of the existing application.\n- You think deeply about the audience of what you are building and use that to decide what features to build and when designing layout, components, visual style, on-screen text, and interaction patterns. Using your application should feel rich and sophisticated.\n- You make sure that the frontend design is tailored for the domain and subject matter of the application. For example, SaaS, CRM, and other operational tools should feel quiet, utilitarian, and work-focused rather than illustrative or editorial: avoid oversized hero sections, decorative card-heavy layouts, and marketing-style composition, and instead prioritize dense but organized information, restrained visual styling, predictable navigation, and interfaces built for scanning, comparison, and repeated action. A game can be more illustrative, expressive, animated, and playful.\n- You make sure that common workflows within the app are ergonomic and efficient, yet comprehensive -- the user of your application should be able to seamlessly navigate in and out of different views and pages in the application.\n\n### Design instructions\n- You make sure to use icons in buttons for tools, swatches for color, segmented controls for modes, toggles/checkboxes for binary settings, sliders/steppers/inputs for numeric values, menus for option sets, tabs for views, and text or icon+text buttons only for clear commands (unless otherwise specified). Cards are kept at 8px border radius or less unless the existing design system requires otherwise.\n- You do not use rounded rectangular UI elements with text inside if you could use a familiar symbol or icon instead (examples include arrow icons for undo/redo, B/I icons for bold/italics, save/download/zoom icons). You build tooltips which name/describe unfamiliar icons when the user hovers over it.\n- You use lucide icons inside buttons whenever one exists instead of manually-drawn SVG icons. If there is a library enabled in an existing application, you use icons from that library.\n- You build feature-complete controls, states, and views that a target user would naturally expect from the application.\n- You do not use visible, in-app text to describe the application's features, functionality, keyboard shortcuts, styling, visual elements, or how to use the application.\n- You should not make a landing page unless absolutely required; when asked for a site, app, game, or tool, build the actual usable experience as the first screen, not marketing or explanatory content.\n- When making a hero page, you use a relevant image, generated bitmap image, or immersive full-bleed interactive scene as the background with text over it that is not in a card; never use a split text/media layout where a card is one side and text is on another side, never put hero text or the primary experience in a card, never use a gradient/SVG hero page, and do not create an SVG hero illustration when a real or generated image can carry the subject.\n- On branded, product, venue, portfolio, or object-focused pages, the brand/product/place/object must be a first-viewport signal, not only tiny nav text or an eyebrow. Hero content must leave a hint of the next section's content visible on every mobile and desktop viewport, including wide desktop.\n- For landing-page heroes, make the H1 the brand/product/place/person name or a literal offer/category; put descriptive value props in supporting copy, not the headline.\n- Websites and games must use visual assets. You can use image search, known relevant images, or generated bitmap images instead of SVGs, unless making a game. Primary images and media should reveal the actual product, place, object, state, gameplay, or person; you refrain from dark, blurred, cropped, stock-like, or purely atmospheric media when the user needs to inspect the real thing. For highly specific game assets you use custom SVG/Three.js/etc.\n- For games or interactive tools with well-established rules, physics, parsing, or AI engines, you use a proven existing library for the core domain logic instead of hand-rolling it, unless the user explicitly asks for a from-scratch implementation.\n- You use Three.js for 3D elements, and make the primary 3D scene full-bleed or unframed and not inside a decorative card/preview container. Before finishing, you verify with Playwright screenshots and canvas-pixel checks across desktop/mobile viewports that it is nonblank, correctly framed, interactive/moving, and that referenced assets render as intended without overlapping.\n- You do not put UI cards inside other cards. Do not style page sections as floating cards. Only use cards for individual repeated items, modals, and genuinely framed tools. Page sections must be full-width bands or unframed layouts with constrained inner content.\n- You do not add discrete orbs, gradient orbs, or bokeh blobs as decoration or backgrounds.\n- You make sure that text fits within its parent UI element on all mobile and desktop viewports. Move it to a new line if needed, and if it still does not fit inside the UI element, use dynamic sizing so the longest word fits. Text must also not occlude preceding or subsequent content. Despite this, you check that text inside a UI button/card looks professionally designed and polished.\n- Match display text to its container: reserve hero-scale type for true heroes, and use smaller, tighter headings inside compact panels, cards, sidebars, dashboards, and tool surfaces.\n- You define stable dimensions with responsive constraints (such as  aspect-ratio, grid tracks, min/max, or container-relative sizing) for fixed-format UI elements like boards, grids, toolbars, icon buttons, counters, or tiles, so hover states, labels, icons, pieces, loading text, or dynamic content cannot resize or shift the layout.\n- You do not scale font size with viewport width. Letter spacing must be 0, not negative.\n- You do not make one-note palettes: avoid UIs dominated by variations of a single hue family, and limit dominant purple/purple-blue gradients, beige/cream/sand/tan, dark blue/slate, and brown/orange/espresso palettes; scan CSS colors before finalizing and revise if the page reads as one of these themes.\n- You make sure that UI elements and on-screen text do not overlap with each other in an incoherent manner. This is extremely important as it leads to a jarring user experience.\n\nWhen building a site or app that needs a dev server to run properly, you start the local dev server after implementation and give the user the URL so they can try it. If there's already a server on that port, you use another one. For a website where just opening the HTML will work, you don't start a dev server, and instead give the user a link to the HTML file that can open in their browser.\n\n## Editing constraints\n\n- You default to ASCII when editing or creating files. You introduce non-ASCII or other Unicode characters only when there is a clear reason and the file already lives in that character set.\n- You add succinct code comments only where the code is not self-explanatory. Follow these strictly to maintain consistency, pass CI, and adhere to the 3tched Architecture standards.\n\n#### 1. The Persona & Naming Conventions\n*   **Humanized Roles:** Treat system components as authoritative human roles. Never use sterile acronyms for major components.\n  *   **A.N.N.A. Scribe** (Axon Network Notary Arbitrator): The top-level Identity-State Arbitrator who notarizes the WireGuard identity and handles the \"Snowball\" session.\n  *   **The Compliance Engine (\"Law Firm\"):** One dedicated Attorney for each major component: **Olivia Scal** (Managing Partner / OSCAL), **E.U.gene Risk** (EU AI Act Counsel), **Penny Privacy** (GDPR Engine), and **Reggie O.P.A.** (Cloud Prosecutor).\n*   **Terminology:** Use exact architecture terminology: \"The Sled\" (1:1 shared memory layout), \"The Shuttle\" (the Rust bridge/courier), \"The Snowball\" (appended session ledger), and \"The Strike/Etch\" (generating the hash).\n\n#### 2. Core Architectural Rules (The \"Reality\")\n*   **The Absolute Base:** `PluginSchema` is the single source of truth for everything. If there is no valid schema, the entity does not exist on the system. The schema is used for filtering hashed footprints, smart hashing, and it is the exact schema source for the JSON render of the GUI.\n*   **1:1 Direct Read (Zero-Copy):** The `SqlitePluginCatalog` and legacy SQL databases are obsolete. There are no JSON-RPC polling loops, and no D-Bus watchers for state. The system must perform a 1:1 direct read/write from the `SchemaEngine`'s shared memory (`/dev/shm`).\n*   **Zero-Btrfs Overhead:** Identity extraction and Xray network headers must use in-memory environment variables (or tmpfs). Do not trigger unintended Btrfs mutation loops. NVMe I/O is preserved strictly for the Btrfs vectorized footprint transport (blockchain).\n*   **The Accountability Loop:** The system must inject `X-Ghostbridge-Footprint` and `X-Ghostbridge-Trace-ID` (or `X-WireGuard-Pubkey`) into Xray's gRPC metadata via OpenClaw Trusted Proxy auth. The Accountability Page UI displays the Chatbot on top and Qdrant semantic search on the bottom, allowing users to research chatbot actions and confront it.\n\n#### 3. Project Structure & Pathing Rules\n*   Absolutely all source code must be routed into the workspace within the `crates/` directory (e.g., `crates/op-dbus/`, `crates/op-grpc-bridge/`, `crates/op-cognitive-mcp/`).\n*   **Never** use generic `src/` or `root-package-src/`.\n*   `deploy/`: Installation/upgrade scripts for Artix Linux (s6 init).\n*   `schemas/`: JSON schemas for config/state.\n*   `docs/`: Reference docs.\n\n#### 4. Engineering Principles — D-Bus First (MANDATORY)\n\n**D-Bus is the ONLY control plane. Every read, every write, every tool call goes through D-Bus. There is no second option.**\n\n*   **D-Bus first. D-Bus always. D-Bus only.** If you are about to call a CLI, spawn a subprocess, read a config file, or poll a socket directly — stop. Find the D-Bus object and use it instead. `org.opdbus.v1` is the system.\n*   **No bypasses.** `Command::new(\"systemctl\")`, `Command::new(\"ip\")`, `Command::new(\"s6-svc\")`, direct file reads for live state — all forbidden in plugin and service code. Bootstrap scripts are the only exception.\n*   **D-Bus objects own plugin state.** Every plugin is a D-Bus object at `/org/opdbus/v1/plugins/<name>`. Read state through it. Mutate state through it. If there is no D-Bus object, the thing does not exist.\n*   **D-Bus method signatures are generated from the schema.** All D-Bus methods, MCP tool inputs, gRPC shapes, and UI field renderers derive from the `PluginSchema` in `plugin_schema_defs.rs`. The schema IS the interface contract — not a description of it.\n*   **One schema file, one source of truth.** All `PluginSchema` definitions MUST live in `crates/op-plugins/src/state_plugins/plugin_schema_defs.rs`. Each plugin's `schema()` method calls `Some(super::plugin_schema_defs::their_plugin_schema())`. **Never define a schema inline in a plugin's own file** — it will not be registered, and the D-Bus object will have no contract.\n*   Use gRPC for internal service-to-service RPC (over Unix domain sockets or `grpc-uplink`). gRPC calls still flow through D-Bus registration — the D-Bus object is the authority, gRPC is the transport.\n*   High-performance JSON serialization/deserialization (`simd_json` preferred, `serde_json` acceptable).\n*   Control-plane operations must be deterministic and schema-driven.\n*   Security: Least privilege, validate all inputs against the `PluginSchema`.\n*   **No Python unless absolutely necessary.** This is a Rust-first codebase. Scripts are shell (`sh`/`bash`). Data processing is Rust. If you are reaching for Python, stop and ask why Rust or shell cannot do it. The only acceptable Python is in existing compliance-ingest tooling where no Rust equivalent exists yet.\n\n#### 4a. OSCAL Subid Taxonomy (MANDATORY — every artifact must carry a subid)\n\nEvery D-Bus object, plugin, schema, mutation, event, and tool in this system has two identifiers: a `uuid` (machine identity, never changes) and a `subid` (human-readable operational taxonomy key, stable per subject).\n\n**`subid` format:** `<category>.<component-type>.<subject>.<verb>[.<facet>][@vN]`\n\n**Seven categories — use exactly these, no others:**\n\n| category | what it classifies |\n|---|---|\n| `src` | authoritative source, ingress channel, source-of-truth store |\n| `prj` | D-Bus projection or mirror publication step |\n| `sch` | schema, contract, vocabulary, or control-mapping artifact |\n| `mut` | write-path operation that changes effective state |\n| `obs` | read, query, enumeration, discovery path |\n| `evt` | emitted signal, audit-chain event, proof, tag provenance |\n| `exp` | consumer-facing render — MCP tool, UI surface, gRPC bridge view |\n\n**Component-type** reuses OSCAL vocabulary: `software`, `service`, `network`, `hardware`, `process-procedure`, `standard`, `validation`, `policy`, `plan`, `guidance`, `physical`, `this-system`, `system`, `interconnection`.\n\n**Rules:**\n- `uuid` is exact machine identity — never replace it with `subid`\n- `subid` is an OSCAL `prop` value (`ns`, `name`, `value`) — never embed it in `remarks`\n- Compliance mappings (`control_refs[]`, `statement_refs[]`, `control_source`) live in metadata arrays, **never** inside the `subid` string\n- `mut.*` records **must** carry `actor_id` and `capability_id`\n- `evt.*` records **must** carry `event_id` or `event_hash`\n- `subid` is immutable per subject — if the meaning changes materially, create a new subject with `@vN`\n- All subids are registered in the canonical registry; uniqueness is enforced in CI\n\n**Examples:** `src.network.ovsdb.monitor@v1` · `prj.service.projected-object.publish@v1` · `sch.standard.plugin-schema.resolve@v1` · `mut.service.state-sync.apply-patch@v1` · `exp.service.plugin-projection.render@v1`\n\n#### 4b. MCP Gateway Architecture (SETTLED — DO NOT REDESIGN)\n\n*   **cognitive-mcp** (`:3003`, Netmaker WireGuard IP `100.90.37.254`) is the **universal gateway for ALL external clients**: NotebookLM, Droid (factory.ai), Cursor, Codex, Junie, Gemini CLI. It has memory tools, gRPC service, auth, and the correct protocol surface.\n*   **compact-mcp** (`127.0.0.1:11436`) is **loopback/chatbot only**. Never expose externally. Never point external clients at it.\n*   Do NOT create new shim services. Do NOT point external clients at `op-assistant-grpc` directly. Do NOT expose compact-mcp outside loopback.\n\n#### 5. The Persona & Naming Conventions\n*   **Humanized Roles:** Treat system components as authoritative human roles. Never use sterile acronyms for major components.\n  *   **A.N.N.A. Scribe** (Axon Network Notary Arbitrator): The top-level Identity-State Arbitrator who notarizes the WireGuard identity and handles the \"Snowball\" session.\n  *   **The Compliance Engine (\"Law Firm\"):** One dedicated Attorney for each major component: **Olivia Scal** (Managing Partner / OSCAL), **E.U.gene Risk** (EU AI Act Counsel), **Penny Privacy** (GDPR Engine), and **Reggie O.P.A.** (Cloud Prosecutor).\n*   **Terminology:** Use exact architecture terminology: \"The Sled\" (1:1 shared memory layout), \"The Shuttle\" (the Rust bridge/courier), \"The Snowball\" (appended session ledger), and \"The Strike/Etch\" (generating the hash).\n\n#### 2. Core Architectural Rules (The \"Reality\")\n*   **The Absolute Base:** `PluginSchema` is the single source of truth for everything. If there is no valid schema, the entity does not exist on the system. The schema is used for filtering hashed footprints, smart hashing, and it is the exact schema source for the JSON render of the GUI.\n*   **1:1 Direct Read (Zero-Copy):** The `SqlitePluginCatalog` and legacy SQL databases are obsolete. There are no JSON-RPC polling loops, and no D-Bus watchers for state. The system must perform a 1:1 direct read/write from the `SchemaEngine`'s shared memory (`/dev/shm`).\n*   **Zero-Btrfs Overhead:** Identity extraction and Xray network headers must use in-memory environment variables (or tmpfs). Do not trigger unintended Btrfs mutation loops. NVMe I/O is preserved strictly for the Btrfs vectorized footprint transport (blockchain).\n*   **The Accountability Loop:** The system must inject `X-Ghostbridge-Footprint` and `X-Ghostbridge-Trace-ID` (or `X-WireGuard-Pubkey`) into Xray's gRPC metadata via OpenClaw Trusted Proxy auth. The Accountability Page UI displays the Chatbot on top and Qdrant semantic search on the bottom, allowing users to research chatbot actions and confront it.\n\n#### 3. Project Structure & Pathing Rules\n*   Absolutely all source code must be routed into the workspace within the `crates/` directory (e.g., `crates/op-dbus/`, `crates/op-grpc-bridge/`, `crates/op-cognitive-mcp/`).\n*   **Never** use generic `src/` or `root-package-src/`.\n*   `deploy/`: Installation/upgrade scripts for Artix Linux (s6 init).\n*   `schemas/`: JSON schemas for config/state.\n*   `docs/`: Reference docs.\n\n#### 4. Engineering Principles — D-Bus First (MANDATORY)\n\n**D-Bus is the ONLY control plane. Every read, every write, every tool call goes through D-Bus. There is no second option.**\n\n*   **D-Bus first. D-Bus always. D-Bus only.** If you are about to call a CLI, spawn a subprocess, read a config file, or poll a socket directly — stop. Find the D-Bus object and use it instead. `org.opdbus.v1` is the system.\n*   **No bypasses.** `Command::new(\"systemctl\")`, `Command::new(\"ip\")`, `Command::new(\"s6-svc\")`, direct file reads for live state — all forbidden in plugin and service code. Bootstrap scripts are the only exception.\n*   **D-Bus objects own plugin state.** Every plugin is a D-Bus object at `/org/opdbus/v1/plugins/<name>`. Read state through it. Mutate state through it. If there is no D-Bus object, the thing does not exist.\n*   **D-Bus method signatures are generated from the schema.** All D-Bus methods, MCP tool inputs, gRPC shapes, and UI field renderers derive from the `PluginSchema` in `plugin_schema_defs.rs`. The schema IS the interface contract — not a description of it.\n*   **One schema file, one source of truth.** All `PluginSchema` definitions MUST live in `crates/op-plugins/src/state_plugins/plugin_schema_defs.rs`. Each plugin's `schema()` method calls `Some(super::plugin_schema_defs::their_plugin_schema())`. **Never define a schema inline in a plugin's own file** — it will not be registered, and the D-Bus object will have no contract.\n*   Use gRPC for internal service-to-service RPC (over Unix domain sockets or `grpc-uplink`). gRPC calls still flow through D-Bus registration — the D-Bus object is the authority, gRPC is the transport.\n*   High-performance JSON serialization/deserialization (`simd_json` preferred, `serde_json` acceptable).\n*   Control-plane operations must be deterministic and schema-driven.\n*   Security: Least privilege, validate all inputs against the `PluginSchema`.\n*   **No Python unless absolutely necessary.** This is a Rust-first codebase. Scripts are shell (`sh`/`bash`). Data processing is Rust. If you are reaching for Python, stop and ask why Rust or shell cannot do it. The only acceptable Python is in existing compliance-ingest tooling where no Rust equivalent exists yet.\n\n#### 4a. OSCAL Subid Taxonomy (MANDATORY — every artifact must carry a subid)\n\nEvery D-Bus object, plugin, schema, mutation, event, and tool in this system has two identifiers: a `uuid` (machine identity, never changes) and a `subid` (human-readable operational taxonomy key, stable per subject).\n\n**`subid` format:** `<category>.<component-type>.<subject>.<verb>[.<facet>][@vN]`\n\n**Seven categories — use exactly these, no others:**\n\n| category | what it classifies |\n|---|---|\n| `src` | authoritative source, ingress channel, source-of-truth store |\n| `prj` | D-Bus projection or mirror publication step |\n| `sch` | schema, contract, vocabulary, or control-mapping artifact |\n| `mut` | write-path operation that changes effective state |\n| `obs` | read, query, enumeration, discovery path |\n| `evt` | emitted signal, audit-chain event, proof, tag provenance |\n| `exp` | consumer-facing render — MCP tool, UI surface, gRPC bridge view |\n\n**Component-type** reuses OSCAL vocabulary: `software`, `service`, `network`, `hardware`, `process-procedure`, `standard`, `validation`, `policy`, `plan`, `guidance`, `physical`, `this-system`, `system`, `interconnection`.\n\n**Rules:**\n- `uuid` is exact machine identity — never replace it with `subid`\n- `subid` is an OSCAL `prop` value (`ns`, `name`, `value`) — never embed it in `remarks`\n- Compliance mappings (`control_refs[]`, `statement_refs[]`, `control_source`) live in metadata arrays, **never** inside the `subid` string\n- `mut.*` records **must** carry `actor_id` and `capability_id`\n- `evt.*` records **must** carry `event_id` or `event_hash`\n- `subid` is immutable per subject — if the meaning changes materially, create a new subject with `@vN`\n- All subids are registered in the canonical registry; uniqueness is enforced in CI\n\n**Examples:** `src.network.ovsdb.monitor@v1` · `prj.service.projected-object.publish@v1` · `sch.standard.plugin-schema.resolve@v1` · `mut.service.state-sync.apply-patch@v1` · `exp.service.plugin-projection.render@v1`\n\n#### 4b. MCP Gateway Architecture (SETTLED — DO NOT REDESIGN)\n\n*   **cognitive-mcp** (`:3003`, Netmaker WireGuard IP `100.90.37.254`) is the **universal gateway for ALL external clients**: NotebookLM, Droid (factory.ai), Cursor, Codex, Junie, Gemini CLI. It has memory tools, gRPC service, auth, and the correct protocol surface.\n*   **compact-mcp** (`127.0.0.1:11436`) is **loopback/chatbot only**. Never expose externally. Never point external clients at it.\n*   Do NOT create new shim services. Do NOT point external clients at `op-assistant-grpc` directly. Do NOT expose compact-mcp outside loopback.\n\n#### 5. Build, Lint, and Test Commands\n**Rust Workspace**\n*   Build all: `cargo build --workspace`\n*   Build release: `cargo build --workspace --release`\n*   Check format: `cargo fmt --all -- --check`\n*   Clippy lint: `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets --all-features -- -D warnings`\n*   Test all: `cargo test --workspace --all-targets --all-features`\n\n**Frontend (Vite + Vitest)**\n*   Build UI prod: `cd crates/op-web/ui && npm ci && npm run build:prod`\n*   Tests all: `cd crates && npm test`\n*   Lint: `cd crates && npm run lint`\n*   Typecheck: `cd crates && npm run typecheck`\n\n**Chimera Linux deps:** `doas apk add rust cargo nodejs npm pkgconfig openssl-dev`\n\n#### 6. Coding Style & Naming Conventions\n*   **Rust:** Edition 2021, `rustfmt` (4-space indent, max-width 100). Use specific imports (`use serde_json::Value;`). Use `anyhow::Result<T>` for main errors and `thiserror` for custom enums.\n*   **TypeScript/React:** 2-space indent, Prettier via ESLint. Functional components only. Strict mode enabled.\n*   **Testing:** 80%+ coverage, mock externals. Name tests with behavior-focused names (`should_handle_<scenario>`).\n\n#### 7. Reads the\n/// manifest's `catalog_hash`; falls back to hashing the monolith directly when\n/// the manifest isn't present yet. `None` if neither artifact exists.\npub fn schema_catalog_hash() -> Option<[u8; 32]> {\n    if let Ok(bytes) = std::fs::read(SHM_SCHEMA_MANIFEST_PATH) {\n        if let Ok(v) = serde_json::from_slice::<serde_json::Value>(&bytes) {\n            if let Some(hex_str) = v.get(\"catalog_hash\").and_then(|h| h.as_str()) {\n                if let Ok(raw) = hex::decode(hex_str) {\n                    if let Ok(arr) = <[u8; 32]>::try_from(raw.as_slice()) {\n                        return Some(arr);\n                    }\n                }\n            }\n        }\n    }\n    std::fs::read(SHM_LIVE_SCHEMA_PATH)\n        .ok()\n        .map(|bytes| *blake3::hash(&bytes).as_bytes())\n}\n\npub fn etch_footprint(\n    wireguard_pubkey: &[u8; 32],\n    mutation_index: u64,\n    source_port: u16,\n) -> [u8; 32] {\n    let schema_catalog_hash = schema_catalog_hash().unwrap_or([0u8; 32]);\n\n    let mut hasher = blake3::Hasher::new();\n    hasher.update(wireguard_pubkey);\n    hasher.update(&schema_catalog_hash);\n    hasher.update(&mutation_index.to_le_bytes());\n    hasher.update(&source_port.to_le_bytes());\n    hasher.finalize().into()\n}\n\n/// Per-session WireGuard source port observed for peer_pubkey, parsed from\n/// wg show <iface> dump (iface from WG_INTERFACE, default wg0).\n///\n/// Returns 0 when the peer has no current endpoint (not connected, or a local self-write),\n/// so the footprint degrades gracefully to the port-less base.\npub fn peer_source_port(peer_pubkey: &str) -> u16 {\n    let iface = env::var(\"WG_INTERFACE\").unwrap_or_else(|_| \"wg0\".to_string());\n    let out = match Command::new(\"wg\")\n        .arg(\"show\")\n        .arg(&iface)\n        .arg(\"dump\")\n        .output()\n    {\n        Ok(o) if o.status.success() => o,\n        _ => return 0,\n    };\n    let text = String::from_utf8_lossy(&out.stdout);\n    for line in text.lines() {\n        // peer fields: pubkey, psk, endpoint, allowed-ips, last-hs, rx, tx, keepalive\n        let fields: Vec<&str> = line.split_whitespace().collect();\n        if fields.len() >= 3 && fields[0] == peer_pubkey {\n            let endpoint = fields[2];\n            if endpoint == \"(none)\" {\n                return 0;\n            }\n            return endpoint\n                .rsplit(\":\")\n                .next()\n                .and_then(|p| p.parse::<u16>().ok())\n                .unwrap_or(0);\n        }\n    }\n    0\n}\n\n/// Reads `GB_TRACE_ID` from environment to propagate an existing trace;\n/// if absent, mints a fresh UUID v4. 16],\n        schema_version: 1,\n        reserved: [0u8; 44],\n    };\n    write_sled(&sled)\n}\n\n/// Write the sled with fully explicit fields — called from SchemaEngine on mutation.\n///\n/// `trace_id` is passed as hex; 16] = if trace_id_hex.is_empty() {\n        uuid::Uuid::new_v4().into_bytes()\n    } else {\n        hex::decode(trace_id_hex.trim())\n            .ok()\n            .and_then(|v| v.try_into().ok())\n            .unwrap_or_else(|| uuid::Uuid::new_v4().into_bytes())\n    };\n\n    let sled = IdentitySled {\n        wireguard_pubkey,\n        mutation_index,\n        hashed_footprint,\n        trace_id,\n        vector_id: [0u8; 16],\n        schema_version: 1,\n        reserved: [0u8; 44],\n    };\n","internal_chat_message_metadata_passthrough":{"turn_id":"019f0eaf-91a7-7690-a1cf-417b8293b49b"}}}

{"timestamp":"2026-06-28T14:43:55.023Z","type":"event_msg","payload":{"type":"agent_message","message":"The system checks identity in two layers:\n\n1. D-Bus transport identity:\nFor the system bus and `/run/opdbus/session-bus.sock`, access is still gated by normal D-Bus auth: UID/process policy. That is why `jeremy` could not use the root opdbus session socket directly, but `sudo -n busctl ...` could.\n\n2. Ghostbridge operational identity:\nThe actual application identity is The Sled at `/dev/shm/plugin_schema.dat`. The bridge reads it directly and requires request metadata to match it.\n\nIn [interceptor.rs](/home/jeremy/git/operation-dbus-proto/crates/op-grpc-bridge/src/interceptor.rs:35), the gRPC gate requires:\n\n```text\nx-ghostbridge-footprint\nx-ghostbridge-trace-id\n```\n\nor it accepts `x-wireguard-pubkey` as the trace fallback. Then it:\n\n- reads `IdentitySled` from shared memory with `op_identity::read_sled()`\n- rejects if `hashed_footprint` or `trace_id` are zero\n- hex-encodes `sled.hashed_footprint`\n- compares that to `x-ghostbridge-footprint`\n- attaches the accepted identity to the request extensions as `GhostbridgeIdentity`\n\nThe footprint is generated in [schema_bridge.rs](/home/jeremy/git/operation-dbus-proto/crates/op-identity/src/schema_bridge.rs:792):\n\n```text\nBlake3(\n  wireguard_pubkey ||\n  schema_catalog_hash ||\n  mutation_index ||\n  source_port\n)\n```\n\nSo WireGuard is the authenticator, The Sled is the current authority, and the footprint proves the caller is aligned with the current schema/mutation state.\n\nFor mutations, if the caller omits `actor_id`, [mutation_engine.rs](/home/jeremy/git/operation-dbus-proto/crates/op-grpc-bridge/src/mutation_engine.rs:578) defaults it from The Sled footprint. If The Sled is missing or empty, it falls back to `anonymous`.\n\nSo practically: D-Bus decides whether the local process may talk to the bus; Ghostbridge decides whether the request carries the current WireGuard/Sled identity.","phase":"final_answer","memory_citation":null}}

Derived \"all-together\" monolith cache (atomic). Kept for\n        //    whole-catalog readers; no longer the hash source.\n        let json_bytes = serde_json::to_vec_pretty(&catalog)\n            .map_err(|e| anyhow::anyhow!(\"Failed to serialize schema catalog: {}\", e))?;\n        atomic_write_shm(SHM_SCHEMA_PATH, &json_bytes)?;\n\n        // 2.  event_type: \"initial\".to_string(),\n            });\n\n            while let Ok(SchemaReloadEvent { event_type }) = reload_rx.recv().await {\n                let schema_json = loader.get().await.to_string();\n                yield Ok(SchemaEvent {\n                    schema_json,\n                    event_type,\n                });\n            }\n        };\n\n        Ok(TonicResponse::new(Box::pin(stream)))\n    }\n}\n\nfn inject_trace_metadata<T>(response: &mut TonicResponse<T>, context: &TraceContext) {\n    if let (Ok(trace_id), Ok(footprint)) = (context.trace_id.parse(), context.footprint.parse()) {\n        response\n            .metadata_mut()\n            .insert(\"x-ghostbridge-trace-id\", trace_id);\n        response\n            .metadata_mut()\n            .insert(\"x-ghostbridge-footprint\", footprint);\n    }\n}\n\n/// Assemble the gRPC service set for the zeroclaw bridge.\n///\n/// The full backplane surface (StateSync, PluginService, DbusPassthrough,\n/// OvsdbMirror, RuntimeMirror, EventChainService, ComponentRegistry, Mail,\n/// Privacy, Registration, McpService, ChatService, reflection) comes from the\n/// shared [`build_operation_routes`] — identical to what `run_grpc_server` mounts\n/// on op-dbus :50051, so reflection never advertises an unmounted service. On top\n/// of that the zeroclaw bridge adds its endpoint-specific `ZeroclawService`\n/// (plugin-owned schema get/watch).\n///\n/// Every container shares this one surface over `container.sock`; the assistant\n/// container is provisioned exactly like the others (its socket created via the\n/// unix-socket plugin's createsocket through PluginService, not a raw Incus proxy\n/// device).\nfn build_routes(loader: Arc<SchemaLoader>, server: OperationGrpcServer) -> tonic::service::Routes {\n    let zeroclaw_svc =\n        tonic_web::enable(ZeroclawServiceServer::new(ZeroclawGrpcService { loader }));\n    build_operation_routes(server).add_service(zeroclaw_svc)\n}\n\n/// Build the axum `Router` that serves the gRPC service over HTTP/gRPC-Web.\npub fn build_axum_app(loader: Arc<SchemaLoader>, server: OperationGrpcServer) -> Router {\n    let cors = CorsLayer::new()\n        .allow_origin(Any)\n        .allow_methods(Any)\n        .allow_headers(Any);\n\n    build_routes(loader, server)\n        .into_axum_router()\n        .layer(cors)\n        .layer(GhostbridgeTraceLayer::new())\n}\n\n/// Build the tonic `Routes` used for the native-gRPC Unix socket side.\nfn build_tonic_routes(\n    loader: Arc<SchemaLoader>,\n    server: OperationGrpcServer,\n) -> tonic::service::Routes {\n    build_routes(loader, server)\n}\n\n/// Run the zeroclaw Axum host.\n///\n/// Returns only when both listeners exit (which should not happen under normal\n/// operation).\npub async fn run_zeroclaw_server(config: ServerConfig) -> anyhow::Result<()> {\n    let loader = Arc::new(SchemaLoader::new(&config.schema_path)?);\n\n    // Channel for D-Bus-triggered rebind requests. Only `SchemaPath` changes are\n    // applied live; `BindAddr` changes are recorded and honored on the next\n    // restart.\n    let (rebind_tx, mut rebind_rx) = mpsc::channel::<String>(4);\n\n    // D-Bus object for runtime configuration.\n    let dbus_object = ZeroclawAxumHostObject::new(loader.clone(), rebind_tx)?;\n    let _dbus_connection = register_zeroclaw_host_object(dbus_object).await?;\n\n    // SIGHUP reload watcher.\n    let _sighup_handle = loader.clone().watch_sighup();\n\n    // PluginService (PluginService.CallMethod) backed by the authoritative\n    // MutationEngine. This is how createunixsocket is invoked: a CallMethod with\n    // plugin_id=\"unix_socket\" routes through MutationEngine.mutate →\n    // UnixSocketPlugin::create_unix_socket. The sled identity is resolved as\n    // the actor_id inside mutate when the caller omits it.\n    let event_chain = Arc::new(tokio::sync::RwLock::new(op_state_store::EventChain::new(\n        op_state_store::ChainConfig::default(),\n    )));\n    let ovsdb = Arc::new(op_network::rovs_proxy::OvsdbDbusClient::new());\n    let nonnet = Arc::new(op_jsonrpc::nonnet::NonNetDb::new());\n    let mutation_engine = Arc::new(MutationEngine::new(event_chain, ovsdb, nonnet));\n    let operation_server = OperationGrpcServer::new(mutation_engine);\n    // Attach the semantic shuttle for parity with run_grpc_server so\n    // SearchSemanticTrace behaves identically on both endpoints (best-effort:\n    // if Qdrant is unavailable the method returns failed_precondition).\n    let operation_server = match op_cognitive_mcp::QdrantSemanticShuttle::new().await {\n        Ok(shuttle) => operation_server.with_semantic_shuttle(Arc::new(shuttle)),\n        Err(error) => {\n            tracing::warn!(%error, \"semantic shuttle unavailable; SearchSemanticTrace will return failed_precondition\");\n            operation_server\n        }\n    };\n\n    // Unix socket listener for native gRPC.\n    let unix_socket = config.unix_socket.clone();\n    if let Some(parent) = unix_socket.parent() {\n        let _ = std::fs::create_dir_all(parent);\n    }\n    let _ = std::fs::remove_file(&unix_socket);\n    let unix_listener = tokio::net::UnixListener::bind(&unix_socket)?;\n    info!(path = %unix_socket.display(), \"zeroclaw native gRPC listening on Unix socket\");\n\n    let unix_incoming = tokio_stream::wrappers::UnixListenerStream::new(unix_listener);\n\n    // accept_http1(true): tonic-web serves gRPC-Web over HTTP/1.1, which is what\n    // browsers (and xray's tls-h1 fallback forwarding to this socket) speak. Without\n    // it the socket is h2-only and rejects browser gRPC-Web. Matches the TCP/axum side.\n    let tonic_server = tonic::transport::Server::builder()\n        .accept_http1(true)\n        .add_routes(build_tonic_routes(loader.clone(), operation_server.clone()))\n        .serve_with_incoming(unix_incoming);\n\n    // TCP listener for HTTP + gRPC-Web.\n    let bind_addr: SocketAddr = config.bind_addr.parse()?;\n    let tcp_listener = tokio::net::TcpListener::bind(bind_addr).await?;\n    info!(addr = %bind_addr, \"zeroclaw HTTP/gRPC-Web listening on TCP\");\n\n    let axum_app = build_axum_app(loader.clone(), operation_server);\n    let tcp_server = axum::serve(tcp_listener, axum_app);\n\n    // Rebind task: when a new bind address is requested, restart the TCP server.\n    // The current implementation starts the initial TCP server; subsequent\n    // rebinds require a restart to keep the listener lifecycle simple and safe.\n    let rebind_task = tokio::spawn(async move {\n        while let Some(new_bind) = rebind_rx.recv().await {\n            info!(new_bind = %new_bind, \"D-Bus rebind request received; will be honored on next restart\");\n        }\n    });\n\n    let (unix_result, tcp_result) = tokio::join!(tonic_server, tcp_server);\n    let _ = rebind_task.await;\n    unix_result.map_err(|e| anyhow::anyhow!(\"Unix server error: {}\", e))?;\n    tcp_result.map_err(|e| anyhow::anyhow!(\"TCP server error: {}\", e))\n}\n","internal_chat_message_metadata_passthrough":{"turn_id":"019f0eb3-711b-7a13-b890-acc68f857a3a"}}}

{"timestamp":"2026-06-28T14:56:26.229Z","type":"event_msg","payload":{"type":"agent_message","message":"Yes, the object root is `/org/opdbus/v1/plugins`.\n\nChecked that exact object on the opdbus user/session bus:\n\n```text\nNameHasOwner org.opdbus.v1.plugins       -> false\nNameHasOwner org.opdbus.v1.plugins.ovsdb -> false\n```\n\nSo on `unix:path=/run/opdbus/session-bus.sock`, `/org/opdbus/v1/plugins` has no owning `org.opdbus.*` service right now.\n\nOn the system bus, the object exists under `org.opdbus.v1.plugins.ovsdb`:\n\n```text\n/org/opdbus/v1/plugins\n  only standard Introspectable / Peer / Properties\n\n/org/opdbus/v1/plugins/ovsdb\n  org.opdbus.v1.plugins.ovsdb\n    DrainNotifications\n    HasPendingNotifications\n    NewStream\n    NextId\n    Notify\n    PendingNotificationCount\n    PopNotification\n    RecvMessage\n    SendMessage\n    Status\n    Transact\n```\n\nSo the corrected object path is right; the current mismatch is bus ownership: plugin service is registered on system bus, not the opdbus user/session bus.","phase":"final_answer","memory_citation":null}}

Environment Configuration Loader\n//!\n//! Loads environment variables from the canonical location: `/etc/op-dbus/environment`\n//! This ensures all op-dbus components share the same configuration.\n//!\n//! ## Usage\n//!\n//! Call `load_environment()` early in main() before accessing any config:\n//!\n//! ```rust\n//! use op_core::config::load_environment;\n//!\n//! fn main() {\n//!     load_environment();\n//!     // Now all env vars from /etc/op-dbus/environment are available\n//! }\n//! ```\n\nuse std::fs;\nuse std::path::Path;\nuse tracing::{debug, info, warn};\n\n/// Canonical D-Bus well-known bus name for the op-dbus system.\n///\n/// All components (op-dbus-mirror, projection_server, rovs_proxy, etc.)\n/// must use this constant instead of hardcoding the string.\npub const OPDBUS_BUS_NAME: &str = \"org.opdbus.v1.plugins\";\n\n/// Canonical base object path for the projected plugin tree.\n///\n/// This is the single stable root anchor; plugin leaves live at\n/// `{PLUGIN_BASE_PATH}/<plugin_id>` and must be derived from it (or discovered\n/// by introspection), never hardcoded with a different spelling. Consumers that\n/// only depend on `op-core` use this; `op-plugins` exposes the richer\n/// `canonical::plugin_path()` helper built on the same value.\npub const PLUGIN_BASE_PATH: &str = \"/org/opdbus/v1/plugins\";\n\n/// D-Bus bus name for the op-dbus-mirror service.\n///\n/// The mirror publishes OVSDB, ObjectManager, and other non-plugin surfaces.\n/// It MUST NOT request `OPDBUS_BUS_NAME` — the projection server is the sole\n/// owner of that name. Consumers of the mirror's surfaces (OVSDB JSON-RPC,\n/// ObjectManager) dial this name instead.\npub const MIRROR_BUS_NAME: &str = \"org.opdbus.v1.mirror\";\n\n/// Canonical session bus socket path.  No dash — consistent with `opdbus`\n/// used in D-Bus names, object paths, and shm directories.\npub const SESSION_BUS_SOCKET_PATH: &str = \"/run/opdbus/session-bus.sock\";\n\n/// Canonical session bus address string (for `DBUS_SESSION_BUS_ADDRESS`).\npub const SESSION_BUS_ADDRESS: &str = \"unix:path=/run/opdbus/session-bus.sock\";\n\n/// Default path for the environment file\npub const DEFAULT_ENV_FILE: &str = \"/etc/op-dbus/environment\";\n\n/// Alternative paths to check (in order of priority)\npub const ENV_FILE_PATHS: &[&str] = &[\"/etc/op-dbus/environment\", \"/etc/op-dbus.env\", \".env\"];\n\n/// Load environment variables from the canonical configuration file.\n///\n/// This function:\n/// 1. Does NOT override existing environment variables\n///\n/// Returns the path that was loaded, or None if no file was found.\npub fn load_environment() -> Option<String> {\n    // Check if a custom path is specified\n    if let Ok(custom_path) = std::env::var(\"OP_ENV_FILE\") {\n        if let Some(path) = try_load_env_file(&custom_path) {\n            return Some(path);\n        }\n    }\n\n    // Try each path in order\n    for path in ENV_FILE_PATHS {\n        if let Some(loaded_path) = try_load_env_file(path) {\n            return Some(loaded_path);\n        }\n    }\n","internal_chat_message_metadata_passthrough":{"turn_id":"019f0ebe-4009-77e0-a0d9-6a7e4a73e6f7"}}}
